title: Learning Spatial Pass Feasibility Under Partial Observability in Soccer
subtitle: Estimating pass feasibility from sparse freeze-frame state tensors
summary: Studied whether interpretable pass probability surfaces can be learned from sparse event-aligned snapshots using structured spatial representations and controlled ablations.

glance.oneLiner: Learning pass-feasibility surfaces from sparse freeze-frame soccer data, with an emphasis on what state representations can support under partial observability.
glance.problem: Broadcast-derived snapshots capture only event-aligned freeze frames, omitting large portions of play, off-screen players, and temporal continuity. This makes pass intent and completion difficult to model reliably and motivates a careful study of which spatial cues are sufficient for meaningful predictions.
glance.approach: Build structured spatial state tensors that combine static geometry priors (boundary/goal distance), dynamic player and ball occupancy, coarse motion summaries, and interaction control maps (Gaussian dominance and nearest-defender distance). Train a fixed two-head fully convolutional model to output destination and completion surfaces, then probe representation choices via controlled ablations.
glance.results: Completion surfaces are coherent and largely stable across feature sets, suggesting local geometry and defender proximity capture much of feasibility. Interaction cues provide subtle improvements in ambiguous scenarios, while destination distributions remain sensitive to representation choices and softmax normalization, limiting conclusiveness.
takeaways: Baseline features capture most pass-feasibility structure in sparse snapshots.
Interaction maps add subtle gains in ambiguous or high-risk situations.
Dense softmax destinations are hard to interpret and can reward overly smooth predictions.
Quantitative metrics alone are insufficient; deeper qualitative study is needed.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Sequential decision-making relies on a state representation that captures the information needed to reason about future outcomes. In fully observable domains like chess, the state is compact and complete. Soccer presents a far more challenging setting. The true state of a match includes continuous player and ball motion, tactical structure, and latent intent, much of which is unobserved or only partially captured by available data.

High-resolution spatiotemporal tracking data can approximate this ideal, but many widely used datasets provide only sparse, event-aligned snapshots. Broadcast-derived freeze-frame data records player and ball locations only at the moment an action occurs, omitting large portions of play and excluding players outside the camera’s field of view. As a result, the effective state available to a model is spatially incomplete and temporally discontinuous, as shown in Figure I.

This project is motivated by earlier work on long-horizon value estimation in soccer, which revealed that learning stability depends critically on what information the state representation can reliably support. Representation gaps and missing context introduced errors that were difficult to diagnose and propagated through downstream value estimates. Rather than treating partial observability as a limitation to be worked around, this work revisits the problem from a more foundational perspective. See the previous project for that earlier study.

Using freeze-frame data from the StatsBomb Open Dataset, we ask how much information is required to recover meaningful spatial structure in passing behavior under incomplete observability. We focus on learning dense pass completion probability surfaces from event-aligned snapshots and study how carefully designed spatial feature channels can compensate for missing players and limited context. Through controlled ablation experiments with a fixed fully convolutional model, this project demonstrates that thoughtful state construction can enable coherent spatial reasoning even in the absence of full spatiotemporal tracking, providing a foundation for future work on decision-making and value estimation in soccer.

callout.label: Key finding
callout.text: Baseline features explain much of pass feasibility; interaction cues help in edge cases, but destination prediction remains inconclusive.

sections.title: Problem Setting and State Representation
paragraphs: We study pass probability estimation from sparse, broadcast-derived soccer data. Given a game state at the moment a pass is taken, we predict a dense surface over the pitch giving completion probability for each destination. Each sample is a spatial tensor $s \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}$ with a binary label at the observed destination cell; supervision is weak because only that cell is labeled.

To make the task identifiable under partial observability, we constrain the pass set before modeling. We keep only completed passes whose end location is within 3 meters of a teammate, which prioritizes short, directly receivable passes where success is governed primarily by local geometry rather than long-horizon intent. Player and ball coordinates are mapped to a fixed $H \times W = 105 \times 68$ grid and all channels normalized to a common range so the model learns comparable scales across cues.

With the supervision target fixed, we define the state in layers, starting with global structure. Static channels encode pitch geometry that is invariant across events: distance-to-boundary maps, distance to the centerline, and goal-oriented encodings such as distance and angle to the attacking goal. These priors provide a consistent spatial scaffold so the model does not need to infer field layout from sparse observations.

We then add dynamic channels for the observable game state at the pass moment, including ball-relative features and binary occupancy maps for attackers and defenders. Because freeze-frame data lacks identity tracking, we use coarse motion summaries from event-to-event displacements: team velocity from centroid shifts and ball velocity from ball displacement. These cues are weak but included to provide directional context without assuming per-player trajectories.

Finally, we introduce explicit interaction cues to bridge the gap between static geometry and sparse dynamics. Two complementary control maps are derived directly from observed player locations: a Gaussian control map and a nearest defender distance map. Both summarize how attacker and defender presence shapes pass feasibility without reconstructing unobserved players or temporal dynamics.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ denote the sets of observed attacker and defender grid locations. The Gaussian control map represents spatial influence by summing isotropic Gaussian kernels centered at each player location, $$A_p(g) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert g-a\rVert_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad D_p(g) = \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert g-d\rVert_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$

These fields provide smooth estimates of attacking and defending presence, but their scale depends on the number and concentration of observed players. We therefore convert them into a relative control estimate via a smoothed dominance ratio, $$\tilde{C}(g) = \frac{A_p(g) + \alpha}{A_p(g) + D_p(g) + 2\alpha + \varepsilon}.$$ This ratio focuses on balance rather than absolute density.

Because freeze-frames often contain large regions with little or no player information, we modulate dominance with a relative evidence weight. We define $$e(g) = \frac{A_p(g) + D_p(g)}{\max_{g'}\big(A_p(g') + D_p(g')\big) + \varepsilon},$$ which measures local player density relative to the most densely observed region in the frame. The per-event normalization ensures $e(g)$ reflects observational support rather than global frequency. The final Gaussian control map interpolates between dominance and a neutral prior, $$C(g) = e(g)\,\tilde{C}(g) + \bigl(1 - e(g)\bigr)\cdot 0.5.$$ This keeps confidence high where observations are dense and conservative where the state is poorly observed.

As a simpler alternative, the nearest defender distance map encodes defensive pressure as the Euclidean distance to the closest observed defender, $$d_{\min}(g) = \min_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \lVert g-d\rVert_2,$$ converted to meters. This representation is robust to missing defenders and provides a sharp local constraint that complements the smoother Gaussian control map.

sections.title: Model and Training Objective
paragraphs: Given a spatial state representation $s \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}$ observed at the moment a pass is taken, the model predicts two dense spatial quantities: (i) a distribution over pass destinations and (ii) the probability that a pass to a given location would be completed. The model outputs destination logits $Z^{\text{dest}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}$ and success logits $Z^{\text{succ}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}$, trained under weak supervision from the observed destination and completion label.

To supervise destination prediction beyond a single cell, we define a smooth target distribution centered at the observed destination $(x^*, y^*)$ using a Gaussian kernel, $$P^*(g) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert g - (x^*, y^*) \rVert_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$ normalized over the $H \times W$ grid. The destination loss is the KL divergence between this target and the predicted distribution, $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{dest}} = \mathrm{KL}\!\left(P^* \,\|\, \mathrm{softmax}(Z^{\text{dest}})\right),$$ encouraging smooth, spatially coherent destination surfaces.

Pass completion is supervised only at the observed destination cell. Let $y \in \{0,1\}$ denote the binary completion label. The success logit at $(x^*, y^*)$ is trained with binary cross-entropy, $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{succ}} = \mathrm{BCE}\!\left(\sigma(Z^{\text{succ}}(x^*, y^*)),\, y\right),$$ modeling the probability of successful reception conditioned on a specific spatial target.

The final objective is a weighted sum of the two losses, $$\mathcal{L} = \lambda_{\text{dest}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{dest}} + \lambda_{\text{succ}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{succ}},$$ with $\lambda_{\text{succ}}$ weighted more heavily to prioritize accurate completion estimates while $\mathcal{L}_{\text{dest}}$ regularizes spatial structure.

All experiments use the same fully convolutional two-head architecture: a shared encoder-decoder trunk with separate prediction heads for destination and success logits. Both heads operate at full spatial resolution, and the architecture is fixed across experiments so differences in behavior are attributable to changes in the input representation rather than model variation.

sections.title: Results and Conclusion
paragraphs: We evaluate models using quantitative metrics and qualitative inspection of predicted probability surfaces. Because the goal is to study spatial representations under partial observability, quantitative metrics serve primarily for controlled comparison and sanity checking, while qualitative analysis is central to interpreting model behavior.

The model separates destination selection from pass completion conditioned on a destination. For completion, we evaluate the predicted probability at the ground-truth destination using negative log-likelihood (Succ@Dest NLL) and area under the ROC curve (Succ@Dest AUC). For destination prediction, we report Dest NLL and Dest Top-10 accuracy. Because destination selection is multi-modal and discretized, these metrics are interpreted cautiously.Quantitative Ablation Results. Table 1 summarizes the ablation study across feature groups.

tables.title: Table 1: Ablation study on the validation set (N=7873). Metrics quantify completion prediction at the ground-truth destination (Succ@Dest) and destination distribution quality (Dest).

afterTableParagraphs: Across most configurations, completion prediction at the ground-truth destination is near saturation. Conditioning on a fixed destination removes much of the uncertainty, so completion reduces to a local geometric problem driven mainly by defender proximity. Differences between feature sets are small, and noticeable degradation appears only when both motion summaries and interaction features are removed, indicating that coarse contextual cues stabilize feasibility in sparse freeze-frame settings.

Destination prediction metrics are higher variance and harder to interpret. In several cases, Dest Top-10 accuracy and Dest NLL improve when interaction features or static channels are removed. These gains do not imply better modeling of pass intent; they reflect the sensitivity of a dense softmax loss to distribution sharpness and multi-modality. Removing features can encourage broader distributions that achieve lower loss without being more realistic. Under these conditions, scalar destination metrics provide only weak grounding and can reward overly smoothed behavior.

We compare predictions across model variants on identical pass events by visualizing completion probability $P(\text{completion}\mid s,g)$, destination distribution $P(\text{dest}\mid s)$, and their product, interpreted as a relative ranking of pass options. The baseline uses ball-relative features plus attacker/defender occupancy, while the final configuration adds static geometry, velocity summaries, and both interaction maps (Gaussian control + nearest-defender). In all figures, the ball is black, attackers blue, defenders orange, and the realized destination red.

Figure VII: Final-model completion surface, destination surface, and their product for the same event.

afterParagraphs: Across a wide range of events, the baseline representation, composed only of ball-relative features and binary player occupancy, produces coherent predictions. Completion probabilities concentrate near viable receivers, implausible regions are suppressed, and destination mass is assigned to a small set of reasonable options. This suggests much of pass feasibility and intent can be captured with minimal spatial cues under partial observability.

Augmenting the baseline with interaction features yields more nuanced behavior in complex situations. For routine passes, predictions remain similar, but in ambiguous or unsuccessful events the enriched model favors destinations with greater separation from defenders or stronger local control. These features improve spatial risk reasoning in counterfactual scenarios.

A limitation of the current formulation is the dense softmax over the full grid. With thousands of cells, even plausible destinations receive very small probabilities, making surfaces appear diffuse and underconfident. The relative structure is informative, but absolute probability scale is difficult to interpret and can obscure distinctions between strong and weak options.

Meaningful and interpretable pass probability surfaces can be learned from sparse broadcast-derived data using carefully designed spatial representations. Simple baseline features capture most feasibility structure, while a small number of interaction features help in complex or ambiguous cases. A key limitation is modeling destination selection with a dense spatial softmax under partial observability; alternative normalization, region-based predictions, or different formulations of pass intent are promising directions. Overall, the analysis is less conclusive than expected and warrants a deeper follow-up study, which I plan to pursue.
